clinicalPearls: Mitochondrial disorder defined by slowly progressive, usually symmetrical bilateral ptosis and weakness of the extraocular muscles, so diplopia is often mild or absent despite marked limitation of gaze.
Most commonly caused by a single large-scale mitochondrial DNA deletion, which is usually sporadic; point mutations and nuclear gene defects are also recognised.
Nuclear genes maintaining mitochondrial DNA — including POLG, POLG2, TWNK (Twinkle), RRM2B and SLC25A4 — cause Mendelian forms with multiple mitochondrial DNA deletions.
Muscle biopsy classically shows ragged-red fibres on Gomori trichrome staining and cytochrome c oxidase-negative fibres, reflecting accumulation of abnormal mitochondria.
Ptosis is often the first sign, with patients compensating through frontalis over-action and a chin-up head posture.
Kearns-Sayre syndrome is a severe early-onset form with pigmentary retinopathy and cardiac conduction disease, and all patients warrant cardiac surveillance.
Management is largely supportive — prisms or strabismus surgery for diplopia and cautious ptosis correction — with vigilance for systemic involvement.
The condition is frequently mistaken for myasthenia gravis, but the deficit is fixed and slowly progressive rather than fatigable and fluctuating.
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia is a mitochondrial cytopathy in which defective oxidative phosphorylation preferentially affects the highly energy-dependent, mitochondria-rich extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae. The commonest molecular cause is a single large-scale deletion of mitochondrial DNA that removes several genes encoding respiratory chain subunits and transfer RNAs; because the deletion generally arises during oogenesis or early embryogenesis it is usually sporadic. Other cases result from mitochondrial DNA point mutations, or from mutations in nuclear genes responsible for maintaining and replicating the mitochondrial genome — such as the polymerase gene POLG, the helicase gene TWNK, RRM2B and the adenine nucleotide translocator SLC25A4 — which lead to secondary accumulation of multiple mitochondrial DNA deletions and follow Mendelian inheritance. Mutant and wild-type genomes coexist within cells (heteroplasmy), and clinical expression depends on the proportion of mutant molecules exceeding a tissue-specific threshold, which is why the abnormality may be abundant in muscle yet scarce or undetectable in blood. Impaired respiratory chain function produces the histological signatures of subsarcolemmal mitochondrial proliferation (ragged-red fibres) and cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, and when the defect extends beyond the eye muscles it gives rise to the multisystem phenotypes of CPEO-plus and Kearns-Sayre syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles or congenital ptosis
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for mitochondrial DNA deletions and point mutations, ideally on muscle, together with a nuclear gene panel (POLG, TWNK, RRM2B and others)
Muscle biopsy with histochemistry for ragged-red and cytochrome c oxidase-negative fibres and respiratory chain enzyme studies
ECG and echocardiography to detect conduction block and cardiomyopathy, essential where Kearns-Sayre syndrome is suspected
Ophthalmological and orthoptic assessment including fundoscopy for pigmentary retinopathy
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies and repetitive nerve stimulation to exclude myasthenia gravis
redFlags: Cardiac conduction block, which can cause sudden death and may require pacing
Onset before adulthood with pigmentary retinopathy, prompting evaluation for Kearns-Sayre syndrome
Systemic features such as ataxia, deafness, diabetes, short stature, dysphagia or cardiomyopathy
Fatigable or fluctuating weakness pointing instead to myasthenia gravis
reference.prognosis: Isolated chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia is relatively benign and progresses slowly over many years, whereas CPEO-plus and Kearns-Sayre syndrome carry significant systemic morbidity and reduced life expectancy, largely from cardiac conduction disease.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as myasthenia gravis and pursuing inappropriate immunotherapy
Failing to perform an ECG and thereby missing potentially fatal cardiac conduction disease
Correcting ptosis too aggressively and risking exposure keratopathy because of weak eyelid closure and an impaired Bell's phenomenon
Relying on a blood sample alone, when a mitochondrial DNA deletion may be detectable only in muscle
Overlooking a nuclear gene cause and the associated family history
